## What is shared (identical across both Shorts)

### Palette — 2–3 colors per image, max

| Role | Hex | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Ground | `#0E3B43` (deep teal-ink) | Field/background |
| Accent | `#F2A541` (warm amber) | The one emphasized word or highlight element |
| Type | `#F7F3E8` (warm off-white) | Caption/title text on the ground |
| Sparing | `#C1543A` (muted clay) | **"The system" framing only — never for blame, never on a parent or child subject** |

Text/ground contrast ≥4.5:1 minimum. `[B]` (Visual brand kit, "Palette")

### Type

One bold sans-serif, two at most. ALL-CAPS reserved for the single accent word. ≥60pt at
1280×720 for any title-card or thumbnail text. `[B]`

**Explicitly out of scope: font availability.** The brand doc's note that the FamilyBrain Pi
compositor currently ships `fonts-dejavu-core` (DejaVu Sans Bold) is a FamilyBrain
infrastructure fact, not a constraint on this project. This run emits Midjourney prompts and an
edit plan for hand assembly — nothing here is composited by braind or any Pi-side system. Do
not import that font constraint, and do not assert which fonts are installed anywhere. `[I]`

### Subject treatment — anonymous human presence

Cleats on a bench, a parent's shoulders on a sideline, hands gripping a fence, a silhouette
against field lights. **Never a host face. Never an empty frame.** `[I]` (this is the brand's
own resolution of the vidIQ-face-vs-1of10-anti-face tension — neither cited source prescribes a
substitute, so it is a brand judgment call, not a sourced rule, per the brand doc's own framing)

### Midjourney consistency mechanism — locked

**`--sref` strategy:** one fixed style code, established once via a **Style Creator** session
run before Short A's first real prompt batch, seeded with the palette/mood description above
(teal ground, amber accent, anonymous-presence framing, muted-clay reserved). Style Creator
sessions are web-only and preview renders consume GPU time, so run previews in `--draft` to keep
the session cheap `[T]`. The resulting code — call it `SREF-RGS-01` in the pool manifest — is
applied via `--sref <code>` to **every** still in both Shorts' pools, Short A and Short B alike.
No second code is created; if a Style Creator session is re-entered later, a new code *stacks*
rather than replacing the first, so once `SREF-RGS-01` is locked, do not re-enter the session
`[T]`.

**Why not `--oref` (Omni Reference):** rejected for the shared system. Omni Reference forces the
job into V7 regardless of the requested version ("adding an Omni Reference will automatically
run the prompt in V7"), accepts exactly one reference image, costs 2× GPU time, and is
incompatible with Draft Mode `[T]`. This pool has no single recurring face or character to lock
— the anonymous-presence rule means every shot's *subject* changes (different cleats, different
fence, different silhouette) while only the *style* must hold constant. `--sref` locks style
without the V7 fallback or the one-image ceiling; `--oref` solves a different problem than the
one this pool has. `[I]` (applying the verified `[T]` trap to this pool's actual requirements)

**Seed discipline:** not one global seed for the whole pool — a single seed reused everywhere
would make every shot look like a re-crop of the same image, defeating the anonymous-presence
variety the brand resolution requires. Instead: **a fixed seed is locked per distinct
prop/subject the first time it is rendered**, and every later still that reuses or varies that
same prop/subject (a different angle on the same cleats-on-a-bench idea, a push-in variant for
the edit) reuses that seed. A new prop/subject gets a new seed. Fixed seeds hold **99% identical**
output on V8.1/8.2 `[T]`, which is what makes a prop's "look" portable across a still and its
edit-plan variants without a second render. Every still's manifest entry (see Still-pool
protocol) records `sref: SREF-RGS-01` and its own `seed: <value>`.

### Caption/overlay treatment

One spec, fixed here for the shared system's visual layer (the full timing/ducking spec is
`shorts-assembly`'s job downstream, per that skill's scope):

- **Position:** captions sit inside the same middle-~60%-vertical safe zone as everything else
  (see Safe zone below) — never in the bottom 25% or right 15%. `[T-unverified]` (inherits the
  safe-zone caveat)
- **Weight:** the one locked bold sans-serif; body captions in `#F7F3E8` on the `#0E3B43` ground
  wherever the shot allows a plate; the single accent word of any given card in `#F2A541`
  ALL-CAPS. `[B]`
- **Reveal timing:** burned-in, revealed at beat boundaries (one caption per script beat, not
  word-by-word karaoke) — consistent with "bold burned-in captions" as a fixed brand rule `[B]`
  and with the brand's one-idea-at-a-time voice trait `[B]`. The corpus has finer-grained
  caption-cadence findings (word-by-word vs. phrase-by-phrase, karaoke-style highlighting) that
  belong to `shorts-assembly`'s edit plan, not this document — flagged rather than duplicated
  here. `[I]`

### Thumbnail layout — locked

Ground field (`#0E3B43`); one amber (`#F2A541`) accent word; anonymous-human subject
right-of-center; 3–5 words of `#F7F3E8` text on the left third; rule of thirds; ≥60pt type at
1280×720; must survive the 120px-wide squint test. `[B]` (Visual brand kit, "Thumbnail rules"
and "Consistency is the actual asset")

### Safe zone — working rule, unverified

All text inside the middle ~60% vertically, clear of the bottom 25% and the right 15%.
**`[T-unverified]`** — no official YouTube safe-zone pixel spec exists; third-party numbers
openly conflict (safe area 888×1500 vs. ~900×1160; bottom reserve 300 vs. 350 vs. 450px; right
120 vs. 150px). Verify on a real phone before committing either Short's template. `[B]` (brand
doc states this same caveat verbatim in its own Shorts section)

## What differs per Short (deliberately)

The system fixes palette, type, and subject treatment. It does **not** fix motif — that is what
keeps the debut pair from reading as the same video twice. `[I]`, applying `[B]`'s "pick one
layout and hold it... change the words, not the system" at the motif layer specifically.

### Motif family A — `decline-the-next-level`

**The escalation ladder, rendered as paperwork and gear.** Registration forms, a pen hovering
over a signature line, a folded uniform on a bench, gear tags/price stickers, a hand pushing a
form back across a table. Traces directly to the grounding brief's visual motif cue: "the same
backyard game shot twice — once loose and self-organized, once run by an adult with a whistle
and a clipboard — cut side by side." `[REF via grounding brief]` (`rgs-briefs/2026-07-28-decline-
the-next-level.md`, Handoff) The motif's job is to make the *offer* — the next tier, the next
signature — a physical, photographable object, so the Short can decline something visible.

### Motif family B — `nobody-asked-the-kid`

**The unwatched moment, rendered as foreground/background.** A standings sheet or scoreboard
held in sharp adult-foreground focus while the actual good moment — a child mid-play, laughing —
happens soft-focused and out of frame behind it. Traces directly to the grounding brief's visual
motif cue: "a child laughing mid-play, coach and scoreboard both out of frame... usable as a
literal two-shot with a standings sheet held in the adult foreground while the actual good
moment happens, unwatched, behind it." `[REF via grounding brief]`
(`rgs-briefs/2026-07-28-nobody-asked-the-kid.md`, Handoff) The motif's job is to make the *gap
between two scoreboards* visible as literal depth-of-field, not just a verbal claim.

The two motifs share nothing structurally — A is object/paperwork-centered (things being signed
or handed over), B is a foreground/background depth composition (things being missed) — which is
what keeps them from converging into the same shot grammar even under one palette and one
`--sref` code. `[I]`

## Still-pool protocol

**Numbering.** Short A's visual stage (Task 12) is the pool's origin. Every still Short A
produces is numbered `A-01`, `A-02`, `A-03`, … in script-beat order, zero-padded to two digits.
Each id is permanent once assigned — a still is never renumbered even if a later still is
dropped, so an id always identifies the same physical asset across the whole pipeline.

**Manifest fields per still (machine-checkable):** `id`, `sref` (must read `SREF-RGS-01` for
every entry), `seed`, `motif_family` (`A` or `B`), `beat` (the script beat it serves), and
`prompt` (the locked Midjourney prompt text). This manifest is what Task 12 produces and Task 18
reads.

**Reuse marking.** Short B's prompt sheet (Task 18) marks **every** shot as exactly one of:
- `REUSE <A-NN>` — points at an existing Short A still id verbatim; no new prompt is written for
  it.
- `NEW <B-NN>` — a Short-B-only still, numbered `B-01`, `B-02`, … in its own beat order, carrying
  its own manifest entry (same `sref: SREF-RGS-01`; a fresh or reused `seed` per the seed
  discipline above).

No third state exists — a shot with neither marking is a spec defect Task 18 must reject before
handoff, which is what makes the protocol machine-checkable (grep the sheet for any shot line
lacking a `REUSE` or `NEW` token).

**Target ratio.** Combined asset count across both Shorts ≈**1.5×** a single Short's count, not
2×. Concretely: if Short A's pool has *N* stills, Short B's prompt sheet should mark **at least
N/2 of its shots `REUSE`** and add **no more than ~N/2 new (`B-NN`) stills**, landing the
combined pool near 1.5N. A Short B sheet where `REUSE` count is less than `NEW` count has missed
the target and should be reworked before Task 18 hands off. `[I]` (arithmetic reading of the
brief's stated target, not a sourced ratio)

## Motion rationing

Image-to-video prompts are reserved for beats that genuinely need motion the edit itself cannot
fake — the **Hook** (first ~2–3 seconds, where the brand's own hook constraint says the visual
and verbal hook both have to land immediately `[B]`) and the **Turn/Payoff climax beat** of each
Short, where the mechanism or the research proof is the moment the video is built around. Every
other beat is a still with movement added in the edit — push-in, parallax, whip cut — specified
in the assembly plan, not rendered as video. `[I]`

This keeps the i2v budget concentrated on the ~2 beats per Short that carry the most narrative
weight (consistent with both grounding briefs' own beat-mapping judgments, which each single out
one beat as doing "the most work" — Dewey's constrained-labor line for Short A, Mason's narration
passage for Short B) rather than spreading motion evenly across a script where most beats are
proof or reframe text that a caption card and a push-in already serve. `[I]`
